question.text: Fund A is described as 'Short-bias Directional', Fund B as 'Dedicated-Long Directional'. How do their NET exposures differ?

answer.text: Both maintain net long exposure; only leverage differs.
Fund A is 100% long; Fund B is 100% short.
Fund A maintains net SHORT exposure; Fund B maintains exclusively LONG positions.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Section 10.1.1.4, Short-bias maintains NET SHORT exposure to the broad market (both long and short positions but net short). Dedicated-Long takes ONLY long positions. They are directional opposites. The Trap: Options A, B and C confuse or invert the definitions — A claims both are net zero, B claims both are net long, and C reverses the positions of Funds A and B. Note: Short-bias and Dedicated-long are both 'directional' strategies under Section 10.1.1.4 but sit on opposite sides of net exposure.
